source: Xu, Peng, Nastase, Chodorow, Wu, Li (2025) Large language models without grounding recover non-sensorimotor but not sensorimotor features of human concepts. Nat Hum Behav
finding: Four LLMs rated about 4,442 words on the Glasgow and Lancaster norm dimensions. Agreement with humans was good for abstract and emotional dimensions, weaker for sensory ones, and minimal for body-action (motor) ones.
numbers: Humans: Glasgow N=829, Lancaster N=3,500. Models: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, PaLM, Gemini; four rounds each. Spearman Rs mostly >0.50 on non-sensorimotor dimensions. Mann-Whitney sensorimotor (n=7) vs non-sensorimotor (n=11): GPT-4 U=65, P=0.018, r_rb=0.69; GPT-3.5 U=67, P=0.010, r_rb=0.74; PaLM U=76, P<0.001, r_rb=0.97.
limits: Ratings are elicited by prompt, not read from internal states. Only 7 sensorimotor dimensions. Vision-training status of GPT-4 and Gemini is inferred from public statements.
agent_relevance: Our agent is text-only. It should not trust its own judgments of bodily or motor properties (how a tool feels, how an action is done); check them against an outside source or a tool.

source: Xu, Peng, Nastase, Chodorow, Wu, Li (2025) Large language models without grounding recover non-sensorimotor but not sensorimotor features of human concepts. Nat Hum Behav
finding: Models with visual training (GPT-4, Gemini) matched humans better than text-only twins (GPT-3.5, PaLM) on dimensions tied to vision, such as imageability and concreteness.
numbers: Visual-association strength from human ratings: imageability Rs=0.69, concreteness Rs=0.62 with the visual dimension; gustatory Rs=0.01, torso Rs=0.02. The gain GPT-4 minus GPT-3.5 and Gemini minus PaLM was set against these strengths.
limits: Pilot analysis. Model pairs differ in size, data and tuning as well as vision, so vision is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Adding image input or a vision tool may help for visual concepts, and probably not for motor or taste concepts.

source: Xu, Peng, Nastase, Chodorow, Wu, Li (2025) Large language models without grounding recover non-sensorimotor but not sensorimotor features of human concepts. Nat Hum Behav
finding: The authors say language gives a partial substitute 'body', like colour knowledge in blind people, but the gap grows toward motor concepts. They propose sensor data and robotics to close it.
numbers: Comparison used dimension-wise correlation and representational similarity analysis across dimensions.
limits: Discussion claim, not a tested intervention.
agent_relevance: Supports a design rule: use language for abstract concept work; add grounding channels only where the task is physical.

source: Marjieh, Sucholutsky, van Rijn, Jacoby, Griffiths (2023) Large language models predict human sensory judgments across six modalities
finding: GPT models given pairwise similarity prompts reproduced human similarity structure in pitch, loudness, colour, consonants, taste and timbre. They recovered the colour wheel and pitch spiral.
numbers: Pearson r with human data: pitch .92 (95% CI .91-.92, GPT-4); loudness .89 (GPT-3.5); colour .89 (GPT-4); consonants .57; taste .54; timbre .42. All above .6 for pitch, loudness, colour. Human split-half reliability: pitch .90, consonants .46, so GPT-4 is near the human ceiling.
quote: lower bound on the amount of perceptual information that can be extracted from language
limits: Similarity judgments are a narrow task. Human reliability caps the score in noisy domains.
agent_relevance: Perceptual structure is more recoverable from text than the strict grounded view predicts. Perceptual relations can be queried from the model as a cheap first pass.

source: Marjieh et al. (2023) Large language models predict human sensory judgments across six modalities
finding: GPT-4, co-trained on vision and language, did not gain a visual-specific advantage. In multilingual colour naming GPT-4 reproduced English versus Russian differences.
numbers: Munsell colour naming: the dominant category (violet) covered 27 colours for GPT-4 and 32 for humans; lilac 20 and 18.
limits: Single examples from the discussion. Tension with the visual-gain pattern in Xu et al. 2025, so vision benefit is task-dependent.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a multimodal model is better grounded on every visual question; test per task.

source: Abdou, Kulmizev, Hershcovich, Frank, Pavlick, Sogaard (2021) Can language models encode perceptual structure without grounding? A case study in color
finding: Text-only LM embeddings of colour terms align with the CIELAB perceptual colour space. Simple co-occurrence (PMI) baselines show some alignment too; big pretraining adds more. Warm colours align better than cool ones.
numbers: Representational similarity: significant correlations in all LM configurations with only 18 colour terms. Linear-map selectivity about .73-.78 versus non-significant shuffled controls. Alignment lower for terms with high collocationality, higher for terms used often as adjectives.
limits: Small stimulus set (18 terms, one language). Static embeddings also align, so the signal sits in text statistics.
agent_relevance: Perceptual structure leaks into text. Weak spots are predictable: terms in fixed phrases carry poorer perceptual information.

source: Zhuang, Fedorenko, Andreas (2024) Visual grounding helps learn word meanings in low-data regimes
finding: Adding visual supervision (CLIP- and GIT-style) improves word learning, but mainly with little training data. With larger data, text-only models catch up or win.
numbers: Benchmarks: syntactic category, lexical relations, semantic features, word similarity, alignment with human neural responses. Visual+Word models were worse than text-only on verb dataset SimVerb-3500 and related colour words differently from humans. Visual models predicted concrete-word features better.
quote: visual supervision can indeed improve the efficiency of word learning. However, these improvements are limited
limits: Reported in figures; per-model scores not extracted. Static-image encoders carry little action information.
agent_relevance: Grounding is a sample-efficiency aid, not a ceiling-raiser. Our agent has huge text pretraining, so extra visual grounding matters mainly for rare or new concepts.

source: Zhuang, Fedorenko, Andreas (2024) Visual grounding helps learn word meanings in low-data regimes
finding: Text and image signals are not redundant: models driven mostly by vision relate words differently from models driven by word co-occurrence. The joint model (GIT) behaves almost like the text-only model, so it mostly ignores vision.
numbers: Correlating judgments between models: Visual+Word (CLIP) differs significantly from Language-only; Visual+Language (GIT) nearly identical to Language-only.
limits: Depends on how the signals are fused.
agent_relevance: Fusing channels can silently collapse to the text channel. Keep channels separate and compare answers; disagreement is information.

source: Li, Nye, Andreas (2021) Implicit representations of meaning in neural language models
finding: In BART and T5 trained on text, contextual word representations encode entity states that update through a story (a simulation-like situation model). A linear probe reads them, and editing them changes generation.
numbers: Intervention (Alchemy, Table 4): after splicing representations, T5 generations consistent with the new state about 75-87% of the time versus about 24-38% for single contexts; BART 58-87%. Probes beat random-init and non-pretrained baselines; example probe accuracy 58.5% and 64.8% at a state declaration.
limits: Toy worlds (Alchemy, TextWorld). Not proof of full perceptual symbols; imperfect, not 100%.
agent_relevance: Text-trained models hold a working state model of situations. An agent can add explicit state tracking (inventory, object state) to reinforce it.

source: Bisk, Holtzman, Thomason, Andreas, Bengio, Chai, Lapata et al. (2020) Experience grounds language
finding: Position paper. Meaning comes from use in a physical and social world. It defines 'World Scopes' from corpus text up to embodied interaction and argues text-only training cannot reach the deeper levels.
numbers: Qualitative; no experiments.
quote: Meaning does not arise from the statistical distribution of words, but from their use by people to communicate.
limits: A position, not a test. Later results (Xu 2025, Marjieh 2023) show text recovers more than expected in some domains.
agent_relevance: Treat the agent as stuck at the text scope. Grounding must come from tools, environments and feedback.

source: Merrill, Goldberg, Schwartz, Smith (2021) Provable limitations of acquiring meaning from ungrounded form
finding: Formal result: assertions in text give enough signal to emulate meaning only for semantically transparent languages. When an expression can have different values in different contexts, emulation can become uncomputable.
numbers: Theorem-level; no empirical numbers.
limits: Applies to the formal model; natural language and learned approximation may differ. The paper discusses this gap.
agent_relevance: Context-dependent words (indexicals, 'here', 'this') are where an ungrounded agent should ask or look, not guess.

source: Mahowald, Ivanova, Blank, Kanwisher, Tenenbaum, Fedorenko (2024) Dissociating language and thought in large language models
finding: Separates formal language competence (rules, patterns) from functional competence (using language in the world). LLMs are strong at the first, patchy at the second and often need fine-tuning or external modules.
numbers: Review; no single effect size.
limits: Review judgement, partly dated by newer models.
agent_relevance: Supports giving the agent external modules (tools, memory, simulators) for world-facing tasks, in line with the scaffold approach.

source: Kramer (2025) Conceptual Metaphor Theory as a Prompting Paradigm for Large Language Models
finding: A prompt asking the model to reason through Lakoff-and-Johnson-style source-to-target mappings was compared with plain prompts on 100 tasks with four small open models. The paper reports CMT beats or matches baseline.
numbers: Models: Llama3.2, Phi3, Gemma2, Mistral. 100 tasks in metaphor interpretation, domain reasoning, explanation, creative insight. Judge: Llama3.3 70B. Results given as figures and prose; no p-values or exact deltas in the text.
limits: Weak evidence. Small models, LLM judge, no human check, no significance tests; authors note unusually high scores suggest evaluation issues.
agent_relevance: The only direct test of a conceptual-metaphor method inside prompting that I found. Treat as untested; if used, only for explanation tasks, with a length-matched control prompt.

source: Liu, van Paridon, Lupyan (2025) Learning about color from language. Commun Psychol
finding: Word embeddings trained on text predict colour-adjective associations (for example yellow-ripe) of both blind and sighted people. Small fiction corpora beat huge corpora and beat GPT-4's elicited ratings.
numbers: Standardised effect (OpenSubtitles embeddings): .60 (95% CI .51-.67) sighted, .21 (95% CI .11-.29) blind. COCA-fiction (120M tokens) outperformed OpenSubtitles (750M) and Common Crawl (600B; different algorithm). GPT-4 rated 10 times at temperature 0.8, plus 500 binary samples per pair at temperature 1.0.
limits: Blind effect is much smaller than sighted, so text only partly explains blind knowledge. Different algorithms confound the corpus-size comparison.
agent_relevance: More text does not mean better sensory knowledge; the type of text (descriptive fiction) matters. Retrieval from descriptive sources might beat asking the model.

source: Liu, van Paridon, Lupyan (2025) Learning about color from language. Commun Psychol
finding: Models learn colour-adjective links from indirect (second-order) co-occurrences, not direct pairing. Corpus-augmentation tests showed which sentences carry the signal.
numbers: Qualitative in abstract and results; ablation sizes not extracted.
limits: Embedding models, not chat LLMs, for the ablations.
agent_relevance: Explains why LLMs can know sensory facts without direct statements: the facts sit in the pattern of neighbours.

source: Conceptual blending in humans and language models (2026) Front Psychol
finding: Conceptual analysis: human blends are goal-driven and built from perceived affordances; LLM blends are novel in distribution but constrained by proxy goals from alignment and prompt framing. A toy vector-symbolic model illustrates the human account.
numbers: Toy Python example only; no behavioural data.
limits: Conceptual paper, not a measured comparison. Author name not captured.
agent_relevance: State the goal explicitly before asking for a blend or new concept, because the goal supplies the constraints that the body supplies in humans.

source: Three-level meta-analysis (2026) Embodied effects in verb processing and learning. Behav Sci
finding: Across 37 studies, embodied effects in verb processing are small but positive and moderated by verb concreteness and verb layer.
numbers: Hedges g = 0.259, p<0.005; 33 independent samples, 265 effect sizes, 12,357 participants. Leave-one-out pooled g 0.22 to 0.33. Fail-safe N 4,903. Publication bias judged small but present.
limits: Mostly Chinese L2 work with mixed tasks (lexical decision, ACE, Stroop). Pools paradigms that failed elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Human embodiment effects are real but small; this caps the weight given to embodiment-inspired designs.

source: Morey, Kaschak, Diez-Alamo, Glenberg, Zwaan, Lakens et al. (2022) A pre-registered, multi-lab non-replication of the action-sentence compatibility effect. Psychon Bull Rev
finding: 18 labs ran a pre-registered replication of Glenberg and Kaschak's ACE. No lab found a reliable effect and the meta-analytic effect was about zero.
numbers: Original: Exp 1 n=35, ACE 155 ms on mean RT 1,766 ms (about 9%); Exp 2a 170 ms on 1,871 ms (about 9%). Replication: 18 labs, meta-analytic estimate essentially zero.
limits: Tests one version of the paradigm. Other action-language effects not covered.
agent_relevance: An LLM comparison to the ACE would test against a human effect that did not replicate; do not use it as a benchmark.

source: Azaad (2026) Studies reporting bodily feedback effects on motivation have poor evidentiary value: a critical review and z-curve analysis. Psychol Res
finding: A z-curve review concludes that bodily-feedback studies on motivation have poor evidentiary value.
numbers: Title-level conclusion; z-curve statistics not extracted.
limits: Scope is motivation effects, not all embodied cognition. Author name as given in the page header.
agent_relevance: Do not build agent rules on posture or facial-feedback priming results.

source: Pavlick (2023) Symbols and grounding in large language models. Phil Trans R Soc A
finding: Not opened. Believed to argue LLM representations can be partly grounded through structural alignment with world models; unverified.
numbers: none
limits: Not read this session; details may be wrong.
agent_relevance: Follow-up only.

source: Patel and Pavlick (2022) Mapping language models to grounded conceptual spaces. ICLR
finding: Not opened (PDF fetch returned HTTP 403). Believed to test whether text-only LMs map to grounded spaces (colours, directions) from few examples; unverified.
numbers: none
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Follow-up; probably close to Abdou et al. 2021.
